title: CPU Scheduling
body:
[[Fairness]]

Deciding which process in the [[Ready Queue]] gets the CPU next. It is the only arrow in
[[Process State]] that the operating system chooses; every other transition is forced on it
by the process or by hardware.

## Preemptive or not

- **Non-preemptive**: once a process is Running it keeps the CPU until it blocks or exits.
  Simple, and one runaway loop hangs the machine.
- **Preemptive**: a timer [[Interrupts|interrupt]] fires, the kernel takes the CPU back and
  puts the process on the back of the ready queue. Needs [[Context Switching]] and needs
  the kernel to be re-entrant, which is where most of the [[Synchronization]] material comes
  from.

## The policies

| Policy | Pick | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| FCFS | front of a [[FIFO]] queue | one long job delays everybody behind it |
| Shortest job first | the shortest next burst | you cannot know the next burst length; long jobs [[Starvation\|starve]] |
| Round robin | front of the queue, run for one time slice, requeue at the back | slice too short and you pay context switches, too long and it degrades to FCFS |
| Priority | highest [[Process Priority]] | starvation, unless you age priorities |
| Multilevel feedback | one queue per priority, processes move between them | lots of knobs to tune |

Round robin plus priority levels is what most of this course means by "the scheduler": one
[[Ready Queue]] per priority, round robin inside a level.

## What you are trading

Throughput, turnaround time, response time, CPU utilisation, and [[Fairness]] cannot all be
maximised at once. Favouring throughput means running whatever finishes soonest, which
starves long jobs. Favouring fairness means slicing finely, which spends time context
switching instead of computing. On a multiprocessor, [[Processor Affinity]] adds a third
pull: the best process to run may not be the best process to run *here*.
